means:
To destroy something **completely and permanently** — to pull it out root and all so it cannot come back.

The word carries totality. *Reduce* and *curb* admit a remainder; **eradicate** claims there is none left to regrow. It also comes loaded with a target: you eradicate diseases, poverty, corruption, pests — almost never something good. And it has a faintly institutional ring, the language of campaigns and five-year plans rather than of one person tidying up.
trick_line: **A radish is a root — er*adic*ate is yanking the root out, so nothing grows back.**
trick_unpack: Cutting the weed off at ground level is *removal*; taking the root is eradication, which is why the word implies permanence and not just absence.
sentences: The commission was charged with **eradicating** the corruption that had grown into every level of the ministry.
You can't just spray the kitchen — you've got to **eradicate** the nest or they're back next week.
in_the_wild: Smallpox is the standard example: the WHO declared it **eradicated** in 1980 — not merely controlled, but gone from the planet. Polio campaigns still use the same word, deliberately.
etymology:
Latin **rādīx, rādīcis** = *"root."* *E-* (out) + *rādīc-* = "root it out."

Same root gives **radical** (going to the root of things), **radish** (the root you eat), and **radix** in maths.
one_line: Wipe out completely, root and all — usually something harmful.
